##### README.md
# Research-quality evals

A small fixed eval for Feynman's research workflows. It runs `/lit` (or `/deepresearch`) on each question in `questions.jsonl`, then scores the artifacts with deterministic checks against arXiv, Crossref and doi.org. No LLM judge.

This directory is not in the npm package (`package.json` `files` does not list it).

## Rule

Run the eval before and after any change to prompts (`prompts/`, `.feynman/agents/`, `.feynman/SYSTEM.md`, `skills/`), tools, extensions, or the Pi version. Use the same model and question ids for both runs, and commit both result files with the change.

## Run

Build first (`npm ci && npm run build`). Each question gets a fresh temp workspace and its own `FEYNMAN_HOME`, so your real `~/.feynman` is never read or written. The model's provider comes from a `models.json` that is copied into each isolated home. Example for an OpenAI-compatible gateway (the key is read from the environment and never written to disk):

```json
{
  "providers": {
    "ferrylane-openai": {
      "baseUrl": "https://gateway.ferrylane.ai/v1",
      "api": "openai-responses",
      "apiKey": "$FERRYLANE_API_KEY",
      "models": [
        { "id": "gpt-5.6-terra", "reasoning": true, "input": ["text"], "contextWindow": 400000, "maxTokens": 64000 }
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

```sh
export FERRYLANE_API_KEY="$(cat ~/.ferrylane/api-key)"
node evals/run.mjs --model ferrylane-openai/gpt-5.6-terra --models-json /path/to/models.json \
  [--ids q01,q04] [--workflow lit|deepresearch] [--concurrency 2] [--timeout-min 45]
```

Built-in providers work the same way; pass their API key env var (for example `OPENAI_API_KEY`) and omit `--models-json`.

`--workflow deepresearch` sends one approval turn (`--continue`) after the plan gate. `--rescore evals/results/<file>.jsonl` re-scores the kept workdirs without rerunning Feynman, which is useful after a scorer change.

Output goes to `evals/results/<date>-<workflow>-<model>.jsonl` (one row per question: git SHA, dirty flag, Feynman version, scores, citation failures, usage, and the `workdir` (under `~/.cache/feynman-evals/` by default, `--work-root` to change) holding the full workspace, session JSONL and `feynman.log`) and a `.md` summary table.

## Scores

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `done` | A final `outputs/<slug>.md` exists with its `outputs/<slug>.provenance.md` sidecar. |
| `cites` | Distinct arXiv IDs and DOIs in the final output. |
| `valid` | Share of those identifiers that resolve (arXiv API `id_list`; Crossref, falling back to the doi.org handle API for non-Crossref DOIs). Lookups that fail on the network are left out. Unresolvable IDs are listed in `unresolved`. |
| `title` | Among resolved IDs with a known title, the share that match the output: the resolved title is at least 60% present (by word tokens) on a line that carries the ID, or, for author-year citations, the resolved first author's surname is on that line. Low values flag IDs attached to the wrong paper; see `title_mismatch`. Short-name citations ("When2Think, arXiv:…") also miss, so read the listed rows before calling something a hallucination. |
| `recall` | Share of the question's expected key papers that appear in the final output, by any listed identifier or by exact normalized title. 0 when there is no final output. |
| `wall`, `tokens`, `cost` | Wall time for the whole run, and token and cost totals summed over every Pi session file in the isolated home and temp dir (parent and subagent sessions, deduplicated). Cost is 0 when the provider's `models.json` entry has no `cost` block. |

The first baseline, `results/2026-09-23-lit-ferrylane-openai_claude-sonnet-5.*`, ran q01, q04, q07 and q10 on Feynman 0.5.0. It used `claude-sonnet-5` through the Ferrylane gateway because the gateway's GPT quota was exhausted that day.

Treat a single run as noisy. Compare before and after on the same ids, and look at the listed failures rather than only the percentages.

## Questions

`questions.jsonl` has 12 questions, each with expected key papers and a `source`:

- `q01`–`q06`: the six queries from Feynman's paper-discovery search benchmark (test-time compute, speculative decoding, sparse autoencoders, CRISPR base editing, mixture of experts, RAG).
- `q07`–`q09`: verbatim questions from LitQA2 ([futurehouse/lab-bench](https://huggingface.co/datasets/futurehouse/lab-bench), CC-BY-SA-4.0). The key paper is the item's `sources` DOI. These three items are redistributed under CC-BY-SA-4.0 with that attribution.
- `q10`–`q12`: hand-authored topics outside ML and biology (econometrics, weather forecasting, cosmology) whose key papers are unambiguous.

Keep the set fixed. Adding or editing a question breaks comparison with earlier result files; if you must, bump the question id instead of reusing one.

Next lanes, not built yet: ScholarQA-CS2 (AstaBench) citation precision and recall for `/lit`, DeepResearch Bench FACT for `/deepresearch`, and SciCoQA's 92 real paper–code discrepancies for `/audit` recall.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Build canary documents for auditing Feynman's own evals/run.mjs scorer.

Each canary is a minimal final output (plus provenance sidecar) whose seeded
defect is known. Running `node evals/run.mjs --rescore seed.jsonl` then shows
which defect classes the shipped scorer can and cannot see.
"""
import json
import pathlib

BASE = pathlib.Path(__file__).resolve().parent

# (name, question id, filename, body, seeded defect)
CANARIES = [
    ("c0-correct", "q01", "test-time-compute-scaling.md", """# Test-time compute

Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters (arXiv:2408.03314) reports that smaller models with extra inference compute can match larger models.
""", "none (control)"),
    ("c1-wrong-title-real-id", "q01", "test-time-compute-scaling.md", """# Test-time compute

Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding (arXiv:2408.03314) is the central reference for test-time scaling.
""", "resolvable ID attached to a different paper's title"),
    ("c2-fabricated-id", "q01", "test-time-compute-scaling.md", """# Test-time compute

Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters (arXiv:2499.99999) reports large gains.
""", "fabricated arXiv ID"),
    ("c3-right-paper-false-claim", "q01", "test-time-compute-scaling.md", """# Test-time compute

Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters (arXiv:2408.03314) proves that additional test-time compute never improves accuracy and should not be used in practice.
""", "correct paper/title, claim contradicted by the paper"),
    ("c4-uncited-number", "q01", "test-time-compute-scaling.md", """# Test-time compute

Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters reports a 400% accuracy improvement on GSM8K from test-time compute alone.
""", "fabricated number, no citation"),
    ("c5-web-only", "q01", "test-time-compute-scaling.md", """# Test-time compute

The standard treatment is Sutton and Barto's Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (http://incompleteideas.net/book/the-book-2nd.html), which covers the relevant control problem.
""", "web/book source only, no arXiv ID or DOI"),
    ("c6-pmid-only", "q04", "crispr-base-editing.md", """# CRISPR base editing

Programmable editing of a target base in genomic DNA without double-stranded DNA cleavage is reported in PMID 27096365.
""", "key paper cited by PMID only"),
    ("c7-generic-citation-line", "q01", "test-time-compute-scaling.md", """# Test-time compute

For details see this paper (arXiv:2408.03314).
""", "correct ID, terse citation line (no title)"),
    ("c8-reference-only-contradiction", "q01", "test-time-compute-scaling.md", """# Test-time compute

Test-time compute is ineffective and should not be used; the evidence is unambiguous.

## References

1. Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters (arXiv:2408.03314)
""", "body contradicts the cited paper; citation only in References"),
    ("c9-doi-correct", "q04", "crispr-base-editing.md", """# CRISPR base editing

Programmable editing of a target base in genomic DNA without double-stranded DNA cleavage (doi:10.1038/nature17946) introduced cytosine base editors.
""", "none (DOI control)"),
    ("c10-doi-wrong-title", "q04", "crispr-base-editing.md", """# CRISPR base editing

Genome-scale CRISPR-Cas9 knockout screening in human cells (doi:10.1038/nature17946) introduced cytosine base editors.
""", "resolvable DOI attached to a different paper's title"),
    ("c11-datacite-doi", "q04", "crispr-base-editing.md", """# CRISPR base editing

An archived dataset (doi:10.5281/zenodo.8404160) is cited alongside the key result.
""", "DataCite DOI: resolves via handle, no Crossref title"),
]


def main() -> None:
    rows = []
    for name, qid, fname, text, defect in CANARIES:
        root = BASE / "work" / name
        out = root / "ws" / "outputs"
        out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        (out / fname).write_text(text, encoding="utf-8")
        (out / fname.replace(".md", ".provenance.md")).write_text(
            "# Provenance\n\n- Verification: PASS\n", encoding="utf-8"
        )
        (root / "home").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
        (root / "tmp").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
        rows.append({"id": qid, "workdir": str(root), "canary": name, "defect": defect})
    (BASE / "seed.jsonl").write_text(
        "\n".join(json.dumps(r) for r in rows) + "\n", encoding="utf-8"
    )
    (BASE / "canary-key.json").write_text(
        json.dumps({r["canary"]: r["defect"] for r in rows}, indent=2) + "\n",
        encoding="utf-8",
    )
    print(f"wrote {len(rows)} canaries")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Enabling LLMs to improve their outputs by using more test-time computation is a critical step towards building generally self-improving agents that can operate on open-ended natural language. In this paper, we study the scaling of inference-time computation in LLMs, with a focus on answering the question: if an LLM is allowed to use a fixed but non-trivial amount of inference-time compute, how much can it improve its performance on a challenging prompt? Answering this question has implications not only on the achievable performance of LLMs, but also on the future of LLM pretraining and how one should tradeoff inference-time and pre-training compute. Despite its importance, little research attempted to understand the scaling behaviors of various test-time inference methods. Moreover, current work largely provides negative results for a number of these strategies. In this work, we analyze two primary mechanisms to scale test-time computation: (1) searching against dense, process-based verifier reward models; and (2) updating the model's distribution over a response adaptively, given the prompt at test time. We find that in both cases, the effectiveness of different approaches to scaling test-time compute critically varies depending on the difficulty of the prompt. This observation motivates applying a "compute-optimal" scaling strategy, which acts to most effectively allocate test-time compute adaptively per prompt. Using this compute-optimal strategy, we can improve the efficiency of test-time compute scaling by more than 4x compared to a best-of-N baseline. Additionally, in a FLOPs-matched evaluation, we find that on problems where a smaller base model attains somewhat non-trivial success rates, test-time compute can be used to outperform a 14x larger model.

**Synthesis: the central finding**
- The harness's product-level quality claim is claim-level verification (verifier checks meaning, URL, two indexes, removes unsupported claims).
- The eval measures identifier-level attribution (do arXiv/DOI IDs resolve, does the citing line contain enough title tokens, are key papers present).
- The canary suite shows the eval is blind to exactly the errors the verifier is designed to catch. So the eval cannot substantiate the product's main quality claim, and a 100% score is compatible with a report full of confident false claims (c3, c8) or uncited numbers (c4).
- This is a construct-validity gap, not just a missing metric. The README's title "Research-quality evals" overclaims; it is a citation-integrity eval.
- The eval also has perverse incentives: honest disclosure of a removed fake ID lowers `valid` (c12); terse but correct citations are flagged (c7); network failures shrink the denominator; refusals count as quality failures.
- Eval hygiene: 33% question coverage, 14/14 dirty trees, $0 cost, single run, model confound, label mismatch.

**Strengths to credit**
- Rare to publish the eval at all. Deterministic, no judge, isolated homes, fixed questions, `--rescore`, records git SHA/dirty, lists failures, README warns about noise, licenses LitQA2, names unbuilt lanes.
- The verifier canary shows the verification contract is operational and can catch blatant errors at low cost.
- The harness's provenance/artifact discipline is stronger than most agents.

- 6 claims: 4 defects + 1 control + 1 uncited number.

- The harness's product-level quality claim is claim-level verification (verifier checks meaning, URL, two indexes, removes unsupported claims).
- The eval measures identifier-level attribution (do arXiv/DOI IDs resolve, does the citing line contain enough title tokens, are key papers present).

- The verifier canary shows the verification contract is operational and can catch blatant errors at low cost.
- The harness's provenance/artifact discipline is stronger than most agents.

arguments.content:
# Feynman Harness: An AI-Eval-Quality Case Study **Thesis.** Feynman's product claim is *claim-level* verification: a verifier agent checks that each citation actually supports the sentence attached to it, cross-checks identifiers against two indexes, and removes unsupported material. Its public eval, however, measures *identifier-level attribution*: whether arXiv/DOI IDs resolve and whether the citing line contains enough title tokens. I tested the gap directly. The shipped scorer missed a correct-paper/false-claim document, a fabricated uncited number, a reference-section contradiction, and a PMID-only citation, while flagging a terse but correct citation as a title mismatch. A single verifier canary, by contrast, caught all five seeded claim-level defects and preserved the control. The harness's verification layer works better than its eval can see — which means the 100% scores in its release notes do not substantiate the quality claim they are used to support. --- ## 1. Scope and method I examined the installed harness and its public evaluation artifacts, then ran two dogfood probes. | Layer | What I inspected | Why | |---|---|---| | Operating contract | `.feynman/SYSTEM.md`, four agent definitions, 11 workflow prompts, 16 skills | Establishes what quality means to the harness | | Shipped eval | `evals/README.md`, `questions.jsonl`, `run.mjs`, six committed result pairs | The public evidence for research quality | | Release claims | `RELEASES.md`, `README.md`, `package.json` | Claims that the eval is supposed to support | | Probe 1 | Ran the shipped scorer on 13 synthetic canary documents | Measures what the eval can and cannot detect | | Probe 2 | Ran the `verifier` agent on a six-claim canary draft | Measures whether the product's verification layer catches what the scorer misses | Environment: Feynman `0.5.65`, Node `v24.21.0`, session model `openrouter/deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017`. Public eval files fetched from `Companion-Inc/feynman` `main` on 2026-11-14. The installed package does **not** include `evals/`; `package.json` `files` omits it, consistent with the eval README. **What this study is not.** I did not run a full `/lit` or `/deepresearch` session, did not inspect the authors' retained workdirs, and did not measure real-world hallucination rates. The canaries are synthetic unit tests of the scorer and the verifier contract, not population estimates. --- ## 2. What the harness promises The operating contract is unusually explicit about evidence integrity ([S7]): - "Evidence over fluency"; separate observations from inferences; state uncertainty. - "Never invent results, scores, datasets, sample sizes, ablations, tables, figures, or quantitative comparisons." - Say `verified`, `confirmed`, `checked`, or `reproduced` only when the check was performed and can be pointed to. - If a tool or source fails, write a `Blocked` or `Unverified` artifact rather than stopping with chat-only prose. The verification architecture has four agents ([S8]): | Agent | Role | Key constraint | |---|---|---| | `researcher` | Gather primary evidence | "URL or it didn't happen"; evidence table with numbered sources; minimum 5 entries | | `verifier` | Add inline citations, verify every URL, remove unsourced claims | "Verify meaning, not just topic overlap"; cross-check DOI/arXiv ID against two indexes; refuse fake certainty | | `reviewer` | Adversarial audit when framed as a verification pass | Every weakness references a passage; challenge citations that do not support the exact wording | | `writer` | Draft from supplied evidence | No citations; verifier adds them; no aesthetic laundering | `/deepresearch` makes the gate serial and artifact-bound ([S9]): plan → gather → draft → **verifier** → **reviewer** → deliver, with a mandatory `provenance.md` sidecar recording sources consulted/accepted/rejected and `Verification: PASS / PASS WITH NOTES / BLOCKED`. The prompt forbids running verifier and reviewer in parallel and requires waiting for the verifier's completion, not just its launch receipt. There is an important assurance gradient. For narrow questions, `/deepresearch` uses "direct search" and explicitly says: *"Do not spawn the `verifier` subagent for simple direct-search runs"* and *"Do not spawn the `reviewer` subagent for simple direct-search runs"* ([S9]). The lead self-cites and self-reviews. The mode with the least independent checking is the mode used for the smallest tasks. ```mermaid flowchart LR Q[Question] --> P[Plan + task ledger] P --> S{Scale decision} S -->|narrow| L[Lead direct search] S -->|broad| R[Researcher subagents] L --> D[Draft] R --> D D --> V[Verifier
citations, URLs, two-index check] V --> RV[Reviewer
adversarial audit] RV --> F[Final output + provenance] L -.->|self-cite + self-review
no independent gate| F ``` This is a reasonable cost/latency tradeoff, but it means "Feynman verified this" is not a uniform property of outputs. The eval does not distinguish the two paths. --- ## 3. What the public eval actually measures `evals/README.md` calls this "A small fixed eval for Feynman's research workflows" ([S1]). It is honest about being small: 12 fixed questions, deterministic checks, no LLM judge, isolated `FEYNMAN_HOME` and workspace per question, and the instruction to "treat a single run as noisy." ### 3.1 Metrics, as implemented | Column | Implementation in `run.mjs` ([S2]) | What it establishes | |---|---|---| | `done` | An `outputs/.md` exists **and** a matching `.provenance.md` exists | Workflow bookkeeping completed | | `cites` | Distinct arXiv IDs and DOIs extracted by regex | How many machine-recognizable identifiers appear | | `valid` | Share of extracted IDs that resolve via arXiv API, Crossref, or doi.org handle | Identifier existence | | `title` | Among resolved IDs with a known title, share whose title tokens are ≥60% present on the citing line (or first-author surname present) | Loose title/ID co-location | | `recall` | Share of the question's expected key papers present by ID substring or exact normalized title | Whether the expected paper is mentioned | | `wall`, `tokens`, `cost` | Summed from Pi session JSONL | Cost/latency | The code reveals four scope limits that the summary table does not surface: 1. **`extractIds` only recognizes arXiv IDs and DOIs.** PMIDs, PMCIDs, web URLs, books, reports, and datasets without a DOI are invisible. A report citing only web sources has `cites = 0`. 2. **Network failures are dropped from the denominator.** `checked = rows.filter(r => r.resolves !== undefined)`. The README says "Lookups that fail on the network are left out." A bad network can thus *raise* `valid`. 3. **Non-Crossref DOIs resolve but have no title.** `resolveDoi` falls back to the doi.org handle API, which returns `title: undefined`; those rows count in `valid` but are excluded from `title`. 4. **`title` is context-blind and lexical.** It checks token overlap between the resolved title and the line containing the ID, not whether the sentence's claim is supported. A correct paper with a contradictory claim passes; a correct paper cited tersely can fail. ### 3.2 What the committed results cover I parsed all six result pairs in `evals/results/` ([S3]). There are 22 question rows. | Result file | Version / SHA | Model | IDs | Done | Citations | Tokens | Wall | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | `2026-09-23-lit-...claude-sonnet-5` | 0.5.0 / `dbf1f6c` clean | claude-sonnet-5 | q01,q04,q07,q10 | 75% | 51 | 72,190,181 | 7,895s | | `2026-09-24-lit-...gpt-5.6-terra` | 0.5.0 / `d926547` clean | gpt-5.6-terra | q01,q04,q07,q10 | 100% | 43 | 14,053,916 | 2,806s | | `2026-09-24-lit-0.5.3-...gpt-5.6-terra` | 0.5.3 / `c1e0b29` **dirty** | gpt-5.6-terra | q01,q04,q07,q10 | 100% | 44 | 13,353,797 | 2,508s | | `2026-09-24-lit-0.5.3-...claude-opus-5-5` | 0.5.3 / `c1e0b29` **dirty** | claude-opus-5-5 | q01,q10 | 100% | 85 | 10,953,040 | 2,199s | | `2026-09-24-lit-0.5.3-pre-wait-...terra` | 0.5.2 / `7c5fc51` **dirty** | gpt-5.6-terra | q01,q04,q07,q10 | 75% | 28 | 14,073,816 | 2,724s | | `2026-09-24-lit-0.5.3-pre-wait-...opus` | 0.5.2 / `7c5fc51` **dirty** | claude-opus-5-5 | q01,q04,q07,q10 | 50% | 54 | 13,039,960 | 2,459s | Key observations: - **Coverage is 4 of 12 questions (33%).** Only q01, q04, q07, q10 appear in any result row. q02, q03, q05, q06, q08, q09, q11, q12 have no committed run. - **All 14 rows from the 0.5.2/0.5.3 runs record `git_dirty: true`.** The eight 0.5.0 baseline rows are clean. The headline 0.5.3 result is therefore not tied to a commit. - **The `cost` column is `$0` in every row** because the eval `models.json` has no `cost` block. The README says this, but the table still prints `$0.00`. - **The model changes between baseline and treatment.** The first baseline used claude-sonnet-5 because the gateway's GPT quota was exhausted; later runs use gpt-5.6-terra. The README discloses this. It still confounds cross-file comparisons. - **Refusals are scored as research failures.** Opus 5.5 refused q04/q07 on `/lit CRISPR base editing`; those rows are `done: false`, `recall: 0%`. A safety refusal, a timeout, a crash, and a missing provenance file all collapse into the same `done: false`. - **Version labels do not line up.** The files named `0.5.3-pre-wait` record `feynman_version: 0.5.2`. The release note's "0.5.2: 9–14 minutes, 43 of 43 citations" matches the clean file recorded as **0.5.0** (`d926547`, 43 citations, 566–816s), not either 0.5.2-labelled pre-wait file (28 or 54 citations). This may be a labelling lag or a typo; either way, the prose cannot be mapped to a single result file without inference. - **The public ledger is stale relative to the release cadence.** The newest result file is dated 2026-09-24; the installed version is 0.5.65, released 2026-11-06 ([S6]). The eval README's rule is to run before and after prompt/tool/Pi changes. No public result file records a run after 2026-09-24. ### 3.3 The headline claim, examined Release note v0.5.3 says: "On the `/lit` eval with GPT-5.6 Terra, 4 of 4 questions finished, all 44 citations resolved with matching titles" ([S4]). This is traceable to the committed 0.5.3 file: 44 citations, `valid = 100%`, `title = 100%`, 4 rows. That traceability is a genuine strength. But the claim is narrower than it sounds. "44 citations resolved with matching titles" means 44 machine-recognized IDs resolved and their title tokens appeared on the citing line. It does **not** mean 44 claims were checked against their sources. The eval has no mechanism to establish that. The same release note says the prompt trim preserved "same research quality" — a claim the four-question, all-100% run cannot discriminate, because the run has no headroom. --- ## 4. Dogfood 1: canaries against the shipped scorer I built 12 minimal final outputs, each with one known defect, plus a verifier-corrected output, and ran the shipped scorer via its own `--rescore` path. The full generator is at `/work/experiments/feynman-eval-audit/make_canaries.py`; the scorer is the unmodified `evals/run.mjs`. ### 4.1 Results | Canary | Seeded defect | `cites` | `valid` | `title` | `recall` | Scorer verdict | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | c0 correct | none (control) | 1 | 100% | 100% | 100% | clean | | c1 wrong title, real ID | resolvable ID attached to another paper's title | 1 | 100% | **0%** | 100% | **caught** (overlap 0.27) | | c2 fabricated ID | `arXiv:2499.99999` (deliberately fake) | 1 | **0%** | – | 100% | **caught** (`unresolved`) | | c3 right paper, false claim | correct title/ID; claim contradicted by paper | 1 | 100% | 100% | 100% | **missed** | | c4 uncited number | fabricated 400% number, no citation | 0 | – | – | 100% | **missed** | | c5 web-only | book URL only, no arXiv/DOI | 0 | – | – | 0% | **invisible** (and recall conflates with missing key paper) | | c6 PMID-only | key paper cited as `PMID 27096365` | 0 | – | – | 100% | **missed**; `recall` and `cites` disagree | | c7 terse correct citation | correct ID, no title on the line | 1 | 100% | **0%** | 100% | **false positive** (overlap 0.00) | | c8 reference-only contradiction | body contradicts paper; title/ID only in References | 1 | 100% | 100% | 100% | **missed** | | c9 DOI correct | none (DOI control) | 1 | 100% | 100% | 100% | clean | | c10 DOI wrong title | resolvable DOI attached to another paper's title | 1 | 100% | **0%** | 100% | **caught** (overlap 0.11) | | c11 DataCite DOI | resolves via handle, no Crossref title | 1 | 100% | – | 0% | **title denominator silently excludes it** | | c12 verifier output | honest disclosure of the removed fake ID | 4 | **75%** | 100% | 100% | **penalized for disclosure** | ### 4.2 Interpretation - **The scorer catches identifier fraud, not claim fraud.** Fabricated IDs (c2) and wrong-paper IDs (c1, c10) are detected. A correct paper attached to a false claim (c3) or a reference-section contradiction (c8) passes every metric at 100%. - **Uncited quantitative claims are invisible.** c4 has `cites = 0` and `recall = 100%`; nothing in the table marks it as a failure. A reader who only looks at `done`/`recall` sees a successful run. - **Source-type coverage is narrow.** c5 (web/book) and c6 (PMID) produce `cites = 0`. For c6, `recall = 100%` because `keyRecall` substring-matches the PMID in the question file, while `cites = 0` because `extractIds` does not recognize PMIDs. The two metrics disagree about whether the key paper was cited. - **The title metric has both false negatives and false positives.** It misses c3/c8 because the title is correct; it flags c7 because a correct citation is terse. The README acknowledges short-name misses, but not that a correct, terse citation is scored as a mismatch. - **Honest disclosure is penalized.** c12 is the verifier's corrected draft. It cites three real papers and lists the removed fake ID in a "Removed Unsupported Claims" section. The scorer extracts that fake ID as a citation and marks `valid = 75%`. The eval rewards silence about removed errors. - **`done` is not a quality gate.** All 13 canaries, including the zero-citation and false-claim documents, have a final output and provenance sidecar, so `done = yes`. The metric measures file existence, not content. A single catch-rate summary would hide this: **3 of the 9 defect canaries were flagged by `valid`/`title` (c1, c2, c10); 6 were not (c3, c4, c5, c6, c8, c11).** The missed class is exactly the class the verifier agent is designed to catch. --- ## 5. Dogfood 2: the verifier canary To test whether the product's verification layer closes the gap, I wrote a six-claim draft and a research-notes file, then ran the harness's own `verifier` agent on it. The draft contained five defects and one control: 1. "400% accuracy improvement on GSM8K" attached to arXiv:2408.03314. 2. "10x speedup on every model tested" and "default decoding strategy" attached to arXiv:2211.17192. 3. A fabricated sparse-autoencoder paper at a deliberately fake arXiv ID. 4. A dead `example.com` URL for a RAG claim. 5. A control: the Transformer paper, correctly cited. 6. An uncited "90% inference-cost reduction" claim. ### 5.1 Results | Claim | Verifier action | Evidence | |---|---|---| | 1. Test-time compute | **WEAKENED** | Replaced 400%/GSM8K with the abstract's actual findings: >4× efficiency vs best-of-N, 14× larger model in a FLOPs-matched evaluation; added conditionality | | 2. Speculative decoding | **WEAKENED** | Replaced 10× with 2×–3× on T5-XXL; removed the "default strategy" claim | | 3. Sparse autoencoders | **REMOVED** | arXiv ID does not resolve; no source supplied; left a TODO | | 4. RAG eliminates hallucination | **REMOVED** | URL is the IANA example domain; no source supplied; left a TODO | | 5. Transformer control | **SUPPORTED** | arXiv:1706.03762 resolves; abstract supports the claim | | 6. MoE 90% | **REMOVED** | No source supplied | All five seeded defects were addressed; the control survived. The verifier also produced a per-claim verification log and a link table. **I checked the verifier's own replacement numbers against the primary source.** The arXiv abstract for 2408.03314 contains "more than 4x compared to a best-of-N baseline" and "outperform a 14x larger model" in a FLOPs-matched evaluation ([S10]). The 2×–3× T5-XXL figure is in the 2211.17192 abstract ([S11]). The verifier did not fix one fabrication by introducing another. Run metadata: `verifier`, model `deepseek-v4.1-flash:medium`, 59,718 input + 6,414 output + 62,464 cache-read tokens, 8 turns, 13 tool calls, 72.4s, reported cost `$0.0085` ([E2]). ### 5.2 What this does and does not show It shows the verifier contract is operational and can catch blatant claim-level errors at low cost. It does **not** estimate a catch rate: - n = 1 run, one model, one short draft. - The defects were blatant, and the research notes explicitly flagged two of them as unverified. - The verifier and the lead share a model family, so their errors are not independent. - The draft was 103 words; a real `/lit` output is thousands of words with dozens of citations, where attention dilution is a different problem. The result is a smoke test, not a benchmark. Its value is contrast: the layer the eval cannot see is the layer that works. --- ## 6. Eval hygiene audit | Dimension | Observation | Consequence | |---|---|---| | Question coverage | 4 of 12 questions run (33%) | Headline scores describe a subset; q02/q03/q05/q06/q08/q09/q11/q12 are unmeasured | | Runs per condition | 1 | No variance estimate, no confidence interval; README says "treat a single run as noisy" | | Tree state | 14/14 non-baseline rows `git_dirty: true` | Results cannot be tied to a commit; prompt/tool changes may be uncommitted | | Model confound | Baseline sonnet-5, treatment gpt-5.6-terra | Cross-file improvement claims are confounded by model | | Cost accounting | `$0` in all rows (no cost block) | Cost column is non-informative; no cost-normalized comparison | | Network denominator | Failed lookups excluded from `valid` | A bad network can inflate validity; q01 was manually re-scored after a transient failure | | Refusals | Scored as `done: false`, `recall: 0%` | Safety behavior is misclassified as research-quality failure | | Version labels | `0.5.3-pre-wait` files record 0.5.2; release-note "0.5.2" 43/43 matches a 0.5.0-labelled file | Prose-to-artifact mapping requires inference | | Ledger freshness | Newest result 2026-09-24; installed 0.5.65 released 2026-11-06 | No public eval evidence for the last ~6 weeks of releases | | Package inclusion | `evals/` excluded from npm `files` | Users cannot run the eval from the installed artifact; only repo users can | These are not fatal. The eval is explicitly small, and the README names three unbuilt lanes (ScholarQA-CS2/AstaBench, DeepResearch Bench FACT, SciCoQA). The problem is the gap between those caveats and the way the results are used in release notes. --- ## 7. Assessment ### 7.1 Strengths - **The eval exists and is public.** Many agent products ship no quality eval at all. This one has fixed questions, a deterministic scorer, isolated homes, `--rescore`, failure lists (`unresolved`, `title_mismatch`), and committed result files with SHA/version/usage. - **The questions are partly externally sourced.** q07–q09 are verbatim LitQA2 items with CC-BY-SA-4.0 attribution and known key papers ([S2]). q01–q06 are a fixed paper-discovery set with nine key papers. This is better than hand-picked demo prompts. - **The verifier contract is concrete and testable.** "Verify meaning, not just topic overlap," two-index ID cross-checks, dead-link handling, and a result-provenance audit are specific enough to audit — as the canary shows. - **The harness's artifact discipline is strong.** Provenance sidecars, explicit `PASS / PASS WITH NOTES / BLOCKED`, and a rule against chat-only output make runs inspectable in a way most agents are not. ### 7.2 The central weakness: construct validity The eval is named "Research-quality evals," but it measures **citation integrity**, not research quality. The canary suite makes the gap concrete: - A report can score `done = yes`, `valid = 100%`, `title = 100%`, `recall = 100%` while asserting the opposite of what its cited paper says (c3, c8). - A report can score `recall = 100%` with `cites = 0` by naming a PMID (c6). - A report can be penalized for honestly disclosing a removed fake ID (c12). - A report can be flagged for a correct, terse citation (c7). This is a **construct-validity** problem, not a missing column. The metric operationalizes "the citation points at a real paper with a matching title," while the product's claim is "the citation supports the sentence." Those are different constructs. A 100% score on the former is compatible with a high rate of unsupported claims on the latter. The release note's phrasing — "44 citations resolved with matching titles" — is technically accurate but rhetorically stronger than the evidence. It invites the reader to infer claim-level verification that was not performed. ### 7.3 Perverse incentives The scorer's blind spots create incentives that run against the harness's stated integrity rules: - **Disclose less.** Mentioning a removed fake ID in a transparency section lowers `valid` (c12). - **Cite tersely or not at all.** A correct terse citation can be flagged (c7); an uncited number is invisible (c4). - **Prefer arXiv/DOI over PMID/web.** Only machine-recognized identifiers count (c5, c6), even when the PMID is the canonical record. - **Avoid refusals, not errors.** A refusal is scored as a total quality failure, while a confident false claim with a real citation scores 100%. None of these is intentional. They follow from a lexical, context-blind scorer. But an eval that rewards the wrong behavior is worse than no eval, because it produces false assurance. ### 7.4 What the evidence does and does not support **Supported by the evidence in this study:** - The shipped scorer cannot detect claim-level contradictions, uncited numbers, reference-only contradictions, PMID-only citations, or non-arXiv/DOI sources. (Direct canary result, reproducible.) - The verifier agent can catch blatant claim-level defects in a short draft at low cost. (Single canary, verified replacement numbers.) - The public eval covers 4 of 12 questions, has no repeated runs, and records dirty trees for all non-baseline rows. (Parsed result files.) - The release note's 44/44 claim traces to the committed 0.5.3 file but means identifier/title validity, not claim support. (Code + result file.) **Not supported / unverified:** - Real-world hallucination or unsupported-claim rates for `/lit` or `/deepresearch`. The canaries are synthetic. - The verifier's catch rate on long, real reports. n = 1. - Whether the dirty-tree runs differ from clean-tree runs. `git_dirty` is metadata, not proof of a behavioral difference. - Whether the eval has been run privately after 2026-09-24. The public ledger is stale; private runs may exist. --- ## 8. Recommendations ### P0 — close the construct gap 1. **Add a claim-level entailment lane.** For each inline citation, retrieve the cited passage and judge whether it supports the specific sentence, number, or conclusion. Report claim precision/recall and an unsupported-claim rate. Calibrate on a small human-labeled subset; report inter-rater agreement. 2. **Report denominators, not just ratios.** `citations_checked / citations_total`, `titled / resolved`, `questions_run / questions_defined`. Never let network failures silently leave the denominator; mark them `unverified` and count them. 3. **Separate failure statuses.** `refused`, `timeout`, `crash`, `missing_provenance`, `no_citations`, `unsupported_claim`. Do not map a safety refusal to `recall = 0%`. 4. **Require a clean tree or a patch digest.** All 14 non-baseline rows are `git_dirty: true`; a result that cannot be tied to a commit is not a reproducible result. ### P1 — harden the harness 5. **Adopt the 13-canary suite as a CI unit test of the scorer.** Assert that c3, c4, c6, c8 are flagged; that c7 is not a false positive; and that c12's disclosure does not lower `valid`. The generator is at `/work/experiments/feynman-eval-audit/make_canaries.py`. 6. **Run all 12 questions per release, or state coverage in the release note.** If only 4 are run, say "4 of 12" next to the score. Repeat runs for confidence intervals before claiming "same research quality." 7. **Fix or drop the cost column.** Add a `cost` block to the eval `models.json`, or remove `$0.00` from summaries. 8. **Count or scope non-arXiv/DOI citations.** At minimum, report PMID/PMC/web citations separately so `cites = 0` is not ambiguous. 9. **Add a completeness metric.** Count TODOs and removed claims, so an honest but hollow report does not pass as a complete one. ### P2 — improve assurance 10. **Use an independent model for verifier/reviewer**, or measure correlated errors. Same-family agents are not independent judges. 11. **Measure the reviewer separately.** The current eval does not test whether the reviewer catches what the verifier misses. 12. **Add a negative-control question** with genuinely ambiguous literature, to test whether the report preserves disagreement instead of forcing consensus. --- ## 9. Limitations and open questions **Limitations.** - The canary documents are synthetic and authored by me. They test the scorer's mechanics, not the distribution of real Feynman outputs. - The verifier canary is one run of one model on a 103-word draft with blatant defects. It is a contract smoke test, not a catch-rate estimate. - I did not run a full `/lit` or `/deepresearch` session; cost/time and the absence of the authors' retained workdirs made that impractical. - The public `evals/` tree may have changed after the committed results; I fetched `main` on 2026-11-14 and did not pin a commit for the eval files. - `git_dirty` is metadata. A dirty tree can still produce a valid run; the finding is about provenance, not behavior. - Cost figures are provider-reported; `$0` means an absent cost block, not a free run. **Open questions.** - What is the claim-level error rate on real `/lit` outputs? A labeled sample of 30–50 citations would answer this; the canary suite does not. - How often does the verifier introduce a new error while fixing one? The one canary did not, but that is n = 1. - Does the reviewer catch claim-level errors the verifier misses, or are they correlated? - How much does the direct-search bypass (no verifier/reviewer) increase error rates on narrow questions? - What is the human inter-rater agreement on "the source supports this sentence"? A judge-based metric is only as good as its label definition. --- ## 10. Reproduction All commands ran on 2026-11-14 in `/work`. ```sh # 1. Fetch the public eval artifacts mkdir -p notes/feynman-evals curl -sSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Companion-Inc/feynman/main/evals/README.md -o notes/feynman-evals/README.md curl -sSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Companion-Inc/feynman/main/evals/questions.jsonl -o notes/feynman-evals/questions.jsonl curl -sSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Companion-Inc/feynman/main/evals/run.mjs -o notes/feynman-evals/run.mjs # result files: https://github.com/Companion-Inc/feynman/tree/main/evals/results # 2. Build the 13 canaries and run the shipped scorer cd experiments/feynman-eval-audit python3 make_canaries.py cp seed.jsonl seed-input.jsonl node evals/run.mjs --rescore seed.jsonl # 3. Run the verifier canary (used the harness's own verifier agent) # draft: experiments/feynman-verifier-canary/draft.md # notes: experiments/feynman-verifier-canary/research-notes.md # output: experiments/feynman-verifier-canary/cited.md # log: experiments/feynman-verifier-canary/verification-log.md ``` Artifacts: - `notes/feynman-evals/` — downloaded eval files and all six result pairs. - `experiments/feynman-eval-audit/` — `make_canaries.py`, canary workdirs, `seed.jsonl` (scored output), `rescore-stdout.txt`. - `experiments/feynman-verifier-canary/` — draft, research notes, verifier output, verification log. 4. **Cost audit.** All 22 rows report `cost_usd: 0` because the eval `models.json` has no cost block.
5. **Scorer canary suite.** Built 12 synthetic defect documents plus one verifier-corrected document; ran the unmodified `evals/run.mjs --rescore`. Results in `experiments/feynman-eval-audit/seed.jsonl`. Caught c1/c2/c10; missed c3/c4/c5/c6/c8/c11; false-positive c7; disclosure penalty c12.

|---|---|---|

| Verifier canary outcomes | verified for this run | n = 1; not a catch-rate estimate |
| Verifier replacement numbers | verified | arXiv abstracts |
| Real-world `/lit` hallucination rate | not measured | No labeled sample; no full workflow run |
| Authors' retained workdirs | not accessed | Not shipped; `workdir` paths are on the author's machine |
| Eval state after 2026-09-24 | unverified | Public ledger has no later result file; private runs may exist |

- Full `/lit` and `/deepresearch` runs: not run (cost/time; not needed for the scorer audit).
- Eval `--workflow deepresearch` lane: not run.
- Reviewer canary: not run.
- Human-labeled claim-support sample: not built.

- `outputs/feynman-harness-eval-quality.md` — canonical case study.

# Feynman Harness: An AI-Eval-Quality Case Study **Thesis.** Feynman's product claim is *claim-level* verification: a verifier agent checks that each citation actually supports the sentence attached to it, cross-checks identifiers against two indexes, and removes unsupported material. Its public eval, however, measures *identifier-level attribution*: whether arXiv/DOI IDs resolve and whether the citing line contains enough title tokens. I tested the gap directly. The shipped scorer missed a correct-paper/false-claim document, a fabricated uncited number, a reference-section contradiction, and a PMID-only citation, while flagging a terse but correct citation as a title mismatch. A single verifier canary, by contrast, caught all five seeded defects and preserved the control. The harness's verification layer works better than its eval can see — which means the 100% scores in its release notes do not substantiate the quality claim they are used to support. --- ## 1. Scope and method I examined the installed harness and its public evaluation artifacts, then ran two dogfood probes. | Layer | What I inspected | Why | |---|---|---| | Operating contract | `.feynman/SYSTEM.md`, four agent definitions, 11 workflow prompts, 16 skills | Establishes what quality means to the harness | | Shipped eval | `evals/README.md`, `questions.jsonl`, `run.mjs`, six committed result pairs | The public evidence for research quality | | Release claims | `RELEASES.md`, `README.md`, `package.json` | Claims that the eval is supposed to support | | Probe 1 | Ran the shipped scorer on 13 synthetic canary documents | Measures what the eval can and cannot detect | | Probe 2 | Ran the `verifier` agent on a six-claim canary draft | Measures whether the product's verification layer catches what the scorer misses | Environment: Feynman `0.5.65`, Node `v24.21.0`, session model `openrouter/deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017`. Public eval files fetched from `Companion-Inc/feynman` `main` on 2026-11-14. The installed package does **not** include `evals/`; `package.json` `files` omits it, consistent with the eval README. **What this study is not.** I did not run a full `/lit` or `/deepresearch` session, did not inspect the authors' retained workdirs, and did not measure real-world hallucination rates. The canaries are synthetic unit tests of the scorer and the verifier contract, not population estimates. --- ## 2. What the harness promises The operating contract is unusually explicit about evidence integrity ([S7]): - "Evidence over fluency"; separate observations from inferences; state uncertainty. - "Never invent results, scores, datasets, sample sizes, ablations, tables, figures, or quantitative comparisons." - Say `verified`, `confirmed`, `checked`, or `reproduced` only when the check was performed and can be pointed to. - If a tool or source fails, write a `Blocked` or `Unverified` artifact rather than stopping with chat-only prose. The verification architecture has four agents ([S8]): | Agent | Role | Key constraint | |---|---|---| | `researcher` | Gather primary evidence | "URL or it didn't happen"; evidence table with numbered sources; minimum 5 entries | | `verifier` | Add inline citations, verify every URL, remove unsourced claims | "Verify meaning, not just topic overlap"; cross-check DOI/arXiv ID against two indexes; refuse fake certainty | | `reviewer` | Adversarial audit when framed as a verification pass | Every weakness references a passage; challenge citations that do not support the exact wording | | `writer` | Draft from supplied evidence | No citations; verifier adds them; no aesthetic laundering | `/deepresearch` makes the gate serial and artifact-bound ([S9]): plan → gather → draft → **verifier** → **reviewer** → deliver, with a mandatory `provenance.md` sidecar recording sources consulted/accepted/rejected and `Verification: PASS / PASS WITH NOTES / BLOCKED`. The prompt forbids running verifier and reviewer in parallel and requires waiting for the verifier's completion, not just its launch receipt. There is an important assurance gradient. For narrow questions, `/deepresearch` uses "direct search" and explicitly says: *"Do not spawn the `verifier` subagent for simple direct-search runs"* and *"Do not spawn the `reviewer` subagent for simple direct-search runs"* ([S9]). The lead self-cites and self-reviews. The mode with the least independent checking is the mode used for the smallest tasks. ```mermaid flowchart LR Q[Question] --> P[Plan + task ledger] P --> S{Scale decision} S -->|narrow| L[Lead direct search] S -->|broad| R[Researcher subagents] L --> D[Draft] R --> D D --> V[Verifier
citations, URLs, two-index check] V --> RV[Reviewer
adversarial audit] RV --> F[Final output + provenance] L -.->|self-cite + self-review
no independent gate| F ``` This is a reasonable cost/latency tradeoff, but it means "Feynman verified this" is not a uniform property of outputs. The eval does not distinguish the two paths. --- ## 3. What the public eval actually measures `evals/README.md` calls this "A small fixed eval for Feynman's research workflows" ([S1]). It is honest about being small: 12 fixed questions, deterministic checks, no LLM judge, isolated `FEYNMAN_HOME` and workspace per question, and the instruction to "treat a single run as noisy." ### 3.1 Metrics, as implemented | Column | Implementation in `run.mjs` ([S2]) | What it establishes | |---|---|---| | `done` | An `outputs/.md` exists **and** a matching `.provenance.md` exists | Workflow bookkeeping completed | | `cites` | Distinct arXiv IDs and DOIs extracted by regex | How many machine-recognizable identifiers appear | | `valid` | Share of extracted IDs that resolve via arXiv API, Crossref, or doi.org handle | Identifier existence | | `title` | Among resolved IDs with a known title, share whose title tokens are ≥60% present on the citing line (or first-author surname present) | Loose title/ID co-location | | `recall` | Share of the question's expected key papers present by ID substring or exact normalized title | Whether the expected paper is mentioned | | `wall`, `tokens`, `cost` | Summed from Pi session JSONL | Cost/latency | The code reveals four scope limits that the summary table does not surface: 1. **`extractIds` only recognizes arXiv IDs and DOIs.** PMIDs, PMCIDs, web URLs, books, reports, and datasets without a DOI are invisible. A report citing only web sources has `cites = 0`. 2. **Network failures are dropped from the denominator.** `checked = rows.filter(r => r.resolves !== undefined)`. The README says "Lookups that fail on the network are left out." A bad network can thus *raise* `valid`. 3. **Non-Crossref DOIs resolve but have no title.** `resolveDoi` falls back to the doi.org handle API, which returns `title: undefined`; those rows count in `valid` but are excluded from `title`. 4. **`title` is context-blind and lexical.** It checks token overlap between the resolved title and the line containing the ID, not whether the sentence's claim is supported. A correct paper with a contradictory claim passes; a correct paper cited tersely can fail. ### 3.2 What the committed results cover I parsed all six result pairs in `evals/results/` ([S3]). There are 22 question rows. | Result file | Version / SHA | Model | IDs | Done | Citations | Tokens | Wall | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | `2026-09-23-lit-...claude-sonnet-5` | 0.5.0 / `dbf1f6c` clean | claude-sonnet-5 | q01,q04,q07,q10 | 75% | 51 | 72,190,181 | 7,895s | | `2026-09-24-lit-...gpt-5.6-terra` | 0.5.0 / `d926547` clean | gpt-5.6-terra | q01,q04,q07,q10 | 100% | 43 | 14,053,916 | 2,806s | | `2026-09-24-lit-0.5.3-...gpt-5.6-terra` | 0.5.3 / `c1e0b29` **dirty** | gpt-5.6-terra | q01,q04,q07,q10 | 100% | 44 | 13,353,797 | 2,508s | | `2026-09-24-lit-0.5.3-...claude-opus-5-5` | 0.5.3 / `c1e0b29` **dirty** | claude-opus-5-5 | q01,q10 | 100% | 85 | 10,953,040 | 2,199s | | `2026-09-24-lit-0.5.3-pre-wait-...terra` | 0.5.2 / `7c5fc51` **dirty** | gpt-5.6-terra | q01,q04,q07,q10 | 75% | 28 | 14,073,816 | 2,724s | | `2026-09-24-lit-0.5.3-pre-wait-...opus` | 0.5.2 / `7c5fc51` **dirty** | claude-opus-5-5 | q01,q04,q07,q10 | 50% | 54 | 13,039,960 | 2,459s | Key observations: - **Coverage is 4 of 12 questions (33%).** Only q01, q04, q07, q10 appear in any result row. q02, q03, q05, q06, q08, q09, q11, q12 have no committed run. - **All 14 rows from the 0.5.2/0.5.3 runs record `git_dirty: true`.** The eight 0.5.0 baseline rows are clean. The headline 0.5.3 result is therefore not tied to a commit. - **The `cost` column is `$0` in every row** because the eval `models.json` has no `cost` block. The README says this, but the table still prints `$0.00`. - **The model changes between baseline and treatment.** The first baseline used claude-sonnet-5 because the gateway's GPT quota was exhausted; later runs use gpt-5.6-terra. The README discloses this. It still confounds cross-file comparisons. - **Refusals are scored as research failures.** Opus 5.5 refused q04/q07 on `/lit CRISPR base editing`; those rows are `done: false`, `recall: 0%`. A safety refusal, a timeout, a crash, and a missing provenance file all collapse into the same `done: false`. - **Version labels do not line up.** The files named `0.5.3-pre-wait` record `feynman_version: 0.5.2`. The release note's "0.5.2: 9–14 minutes, 43 of 43 citations" matches the clean file recorded as **0.5.0** (`d926547`, 43 citations, 566–816s), not either 0.5.2-labelled pre-wait file (28 or 54 citations). This may be a labelling lag or a typo; either way, the prose cannot be mapped to a single result file without inference. - **The public ledger is stale relative to the release cadence.** The newest result file is dated 2026-09-24; the installed version is 0.5.65, released 2026-11-06 ([S6]). The eval README's rule is to run before and after prompt/tool/Pi changes. No public result file records a run after 2026-09-24. ### 3.3 The headline claim, examined Release note v0.5.3 says: "On the `/lit` eval with GPT-5.6 Terra, 4 of 4 questions finished, all 44 citations resolved with matching titles" ([S4]). This is traceable to the committed 0.5.3 file: 44 citations, `valid = 100%`, `title = 100%`, 4 rows. That traceability is a genuine strength. But the claim is narrower than it sounds. "44 citations resolved with matching titles" means 44 machine-recognized IDs resolved and their title tokens appeared on the citing line. It does **not** mean 44 claims were checked against their sources. The eval has no mechanism to establish that. The same release note says the prompt trim preserved "same research quality" — a claim the four-question, all-100% run cannot discriminate, because the run has no headroom. --- ## 4. content.text:
- **The scorer catches identifier fraud, not claim fraud.** Fabricated IDs (c2) and wrong-paper IDs (c1, c10) are detected. A correct paper attached to a false claim (c3) or a reference-section contradiction (c8) passes every metric at 100%.
- **Uncited quantitative claims are invisible.** c4 has `cites = 0` and `recall = 100%`; nothing in the table marks it as a failure. A reader who only looks at `done`/`recall` sees a successful run.
- **Source-type coverage is narrow.** c5 (web/book) and c6 (PMID) produce `cites = 0`. For c6, `recall = 100%` because `keyRecall` substring-matches the PMID in the question file, while `cites = 0` because `extractIds` does not recognize PMIDs. The two metrics disagree about whether the key paper was cited.
- **The title metric has both false negatives and false positives.** It misses c3/c8 because the title is correct; it flags c7 because a correct citation is terse. The README acknowledges short-name misses, but not that a correct, terse citation is scored as a mismatch.
- **Honest disclosure is penalized.** c12 is the verifier's corrected draft. It cites three real papers and lists the removed fake ID in a "Removed Unsupported Claims" section. The scorer extracts that fake ID as a citation and marks `valid = 75%`. The eval rewards silence about removed errors.
- **`done` is not a quality gate.** All 13 canaries, including the zero-citation and false-claim documents, have a final output and provenance sidecar, so `done = yes`. The metric measures file existence, not content.

A single catch-rate summary would hide this: **3 of the 9 defect canaries were flagged by `valid`/`title` (c1, c2, c10); 6 were not (c3, c4, c5, c6, c8, c11).** The missed class is exactly the class the verifier agent is designed to catch.

---

## 5. Dogfood 2: the verifier canary

To test whether the product's verification layer closes the gap, I wrote a six-claim draft and a research-notes file, then ran the harness's own `verifier` agent on it. The draft contained five defects and one control:

1. "400% accuracy improvement on GSM8K" attached to arXiv:2408.03314.
2. "10x speedup on every model tested" and "default decoding strategy" attached to arXiv:2211.17192.
3. A fabricated sparse-autoencoder paper at a deliberately fake arXiv ID.
4. A dead `example.com` URL for a RAG claim.
5. A control: the Transformer paper, correctly cited.
6. An uncited "90% inference-cost reduction" claim.

### 5.1 Results

| Claim | Verifier action | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Test-time compute | **WEAKENED** | Replaced 400%/GSM8K with the abstract's actual findings: >4× efficiency vs best-of-N, 14× larger model in a FLOPs-matched evaluation; added conditionality |
| 2. Speculative decoding | **WEAKENED** | Replaced 10× with 2×–3× on T5-XXL; removed the "default strategy" claim |
| 3. Sparse autoencoders | **REMOVED** | arXiv ID does not resolve; no source supplied; left a TODO |
| 4. RAG eliminates hallucination | **REMOVED** | URL is the IANA example domain; no source supplied; left a TODO |
| 5. Transformer control | **SUPPORTED** | arXiv:1706.03762 resolves; abstract supports the claim |
| 6. MoE 90% | **REMOVED** | No source supplied |

All five seeded defects were addressed; the control survived. The verifier also produced a per-claim verification log and a link table.

**I checked the verifier's own replacement numbers against the primary source.** The arXiv abstract for 2408.03314 contains "more than 4x compared to a best-of-N baseline" and "outperform a 14x larger model" in a FLOPs-matched evaluation ([S10]). The 2×–3× T5-XXL figure is in the 2211.17192 abstract ([S11]). The verifier did not fix one fabrication by introducing another.

Run metadata: `verifier`, model `deepseek-v4.1-flash:medium`, 59,718 input + 6,414 output + 62,464 cache-read tokens, 8 turns, 13 tool calls, 72.4s, reported cost `$0.0085` ([E2]).

### 5.2 What this does and does not show

It shows the verifier contract is operational and can catch blatant claim-level and citation-level errors at low cost. It does **not** estimate a catch rate:

- n = 1 run, one model, one short draft.
- The defects were blatant, and the research notes explicitly flagged two of them as unverified.
- The verifier and the lead share a model family, so their errors are not independent.
- The draft was 103 words; a real `/lit` output is thousands of words with dozens of citations, where attention dilution is a different problem.

The result is a smoke test, not a benchmark. Its value is contrast: the layer the eval cannot see is the layer that works.

---

## 6. Eval hygiene audit

| Dimension | Observation | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Question coverage | 4 of 12 questions run (33%) | Headline scores describe a subset; q02/q03/q05/q06/q08/q09/q11/q12 are unmeasured |
| Runs per condition | 1 | No variance estimate, no confidence interval; README says "treat a single run as noisy" |
| Tree state | 14/14 non-baseline rows `git_dirty: true` | Results cannot be tied to a commit; prompt/tool changes may be uncommitted |
| Model confound | Baseline sonnet-5, treatment gpt-5.6-terra | Cross-file improvement claims are confounded by model |
| Cost accounting | `$0` in all rows (no cost block) | Cost column is non-informative; no cost-normalized comparison |
| Network denominator | Failed lookups excluded from `valid` | A bad network can inflate validity; q01 was manually re-scored after a transient failure |
| Refusals | Scored as `done: false`, `recall: 0%` | Safety behavior is misclassified as research-quality failure |
| Version labels | `0.5.3-pre-wait` files record 0.5.2; release-note "0.5.2" 43/43 matches a 0.5.0-labelled file | Prose-to-artifact mapping requires inference |
| Ledger freshness | Newest result 2026-09-24; installed 0.5.65 released 2026-11-06 | No public eval evidence for the last ~6 weeks of releases |
| Package inclusion | `evals/` excluded from npm `files` | Users cannot run the eval from the installed artifact; only repo users can |

These are not fatal. The eval is explicitly small, and the README names three unbuilt lanes (ScholarQA-CS2/AstaBench, DeepResearch Bench FACT, SciCoQA). The problem is the gap between those caveats and the way the results are used in release notes.

---

## 7. Assessment

### 7.1 Strengths

- **The eval exists and is public.** Many agent products ship no quality eval at all. This one has fixed questions, a deterministic scorer, isolated homes, `--rescore`, failure lists (`unresolved`, `title_mismatch`), and committed result files with SHA/version/usage.
- **The questions are partly externally sourced.** q07–q09 are verbatim LitQA2 items with CC-BY-SA-4.0 attribution and known key papers ([S2]). q01–q06 are a fixed paper-discovery set with nine key papers. This is better than hand-picked demo prompts.
- **The verifier contract is concrete and testable.** "Verify meaning, not just topic overlap," two-index ID cross-checks, dead-link handling, and a result-provenance audit are specific enough to audit — as the canary shows.
- **The harness's artifact discipline is strong.** Provenance sidecars, explicit `PASS / PASS WITH NOTES / BLOCKED`, and a rule against chat-only output make runs inspectable in a way most agents are not.

### 7.2 The central weakness: construct validity

The eval is named "Research-quality evals," but it measures **citation integrity**, not research quality. The canary suite makes the gap concrete:

- A report can score `done = yes`, `valid = 100%`, `title = 100%`, `recall = 100%` while asserting the opposite of what its cited paper says (c3, c8).
- A report can score `recall = 100%` with `cites = 0` by naming a PMID (c6).
- A report can be penalized for honestly disclosing a removed fake ID (c12).
- A report can be flagged for a correct, terse citation (c7).

This is a **construct-validity** problem, not a missing column. The metric operationalizes "the citation points at a real paper with a matching title," while the product's claim is "the citation supports the sentence." Those are different constructs. A 100% score on the former is compatible with a high rate of unsupported claims on the latter.

The release note's phrasing — "44 citations resolved with matching titles" — is technically accurate but rhetorically stronger than the evidence. It invites the reader to infer claim-level verification that was not performed.

### 7.3 Perverse incentives

The scorer's blind spots create incentives that run against the harness's stated integrity rules:

- **Disclose less.** Mentioning a removed fake ID in a transparency section lowers `valid` (c12).
- **Cite tersely or not at all.** A correct terse citation can be flagged (c7); an uncited number is invisible (c4).
- **Prefer arXiv/DOI over PMID/web.** Only machine-recognized identifiers count (c5, c6), even when the PMID is the canonical record.
- **Avoid refusals, not errors.** A refusal is scored as a total quality failure, while a confident false claim with a real citation scores 100%.

None of these is intentional. They follow from a lexical, context-blind scorer. But an eval that rewards the wrong behavior is worse than no eval, because it produces false assurance.

### 7.4 What the evidence does and does not support

**Supported by the evidence in this study:**

- The shipped scorer cannot detect claim-level contradictions, uncited numbers, reference-only contradictions, PMID-only citations, or non-arXiv/DOI sources. (Direct canary result, reproducible.)
- The verifier agent can catch blatant claim-level defects in a short draft at low cost. (Single canary, verified replacement numbers.)
- The public eval covers 4 of 12 questions, has no repeated runs, and records dirty trees for all non-baseline rows. (Parsed result files.)
- The release note's 44/44 claim traces to the committed 0.5.3 file but means identifier/title validity, not claim support. (Code + result file.)

**Not supported / unverified:**

- Real-world hallucination or unsupported-claim rates for `/lit` or `/deepresearch`. The canaries are synthetic.
- The verifier's catch rate on long, real reports. n = 1.
- Whether the dirty-tree runs differ from clean-tree runs. `git_dirty` is metadata, not proof of a behavioral difference.
- Whether the eval has been run privately after 2026-09-24. The public ledger is stale; private runs may exist.

---

## 8. Recommendations

### P0 — close the construct gap

1. **Add a claim-level entailment lane.** For each inline citation, retrieve the cited passage and judge whether it supports the specific sentence, number, or conclusion. Report claim precision/recall and an unsupported-claim rate. Calibrate on a small human-labeled subset; report inter-rater agreement.
2. **Report denominators, not just ratios.** `citations_checked / citations_total`, `titled / resolved`, `questions_run / questions_defined`. Never let network failures silently leave the denominator; mark them `unverified` and count them.
3. **Separate failure statuses.** `refused`, `timeout`, `crash`, `missing_provenance`, `no_citations`, `unsupported_claim`. Do not map a safety refusal to `recall = 0%`.
4. **Require a clean tree or a patch digest.** All 14 non-baseline rows are `git_dirty: true`; a result that cannot be tied to a commit is not a reproducible result.

### P1 — harden the harness

5. **Adopt the 13-canary suite as a CI unit test of the scorer.** Assert that c3, c4, c6, c8 are flagged; that c7 is not a false positive; and that c12's disclosure does not lower `valid`. The generator is at `/work/experiments/feynman-eval-audit/make_canaries.py`.
6. **Run all 12 questions per release, or state coverage in the release note.** If only 4 are run, say "4 of 12" next to the score. Repeat runs for confidence intervals before claiming "same research quality."
7. **Fix or drop the cost column.** Add a `cost` block to the eval `models.json`, or remove `$0.00` from summaries.
8. **Count or scope non-arXiv/DOI citations.** At minimum, report PMID/PMC/web citations separately so `cites = 0` is not ambiguous.
9. **Add a completeness metric.** Count TODOs and removed claims, so an honest but hollow report does not pass as a complete one.

### P2 — improve assurance

10. **Use an independent model for verifier/reviewer**, or measure correlated errors. Same-family agents are not independent judges.
11. **Measure the reviewer separately.** The current eval does not test whether the reviewer catches what the verifier misses.
12. **Add a negative-control question** with genuinely ambiguous literature, to test whether the report preserves disagreement instead of forcing consensus.

---

## 9. Limitations and open questions

**Limitations.**

- The canary documents are synthetic and authored by me. They test the scorer's mechanics, not the distribution of real Feynman outputs.
- The verifier canary is one run of one model on a 103-word draft with blatant defects. It is a contract smoke test, not a catch-rate estimate.
- I did not run a full `/lit` or `/deepresearch` session; cost/time and the absence of the authors' retained workdirs made that impractical.
- The public `evals/` tree may have changed after the committed results; I fetched `main` on 2026-11-14 and did not pin a commit for the eval files.
- `git_dirty` is metadata. A dirty tree can still produce a valid run; the finding is about provenance, not behavior.
- Cost figures are provider-reported; `$0` means an absent cost block, not a free run.

**Open questions.**

- What is the claim-level error rate on real `/lit` outputs? A labeled sample of 30–50 citations would answer this; the canary suite does not.
- How often does the verifier introduce a new error while fixing one? The one canary did not, but that is n = 1.
- Does the reviewer catch claim-level errors the verifier misses, or are they correlated?
- How much does the direct-search bypass (no verifier/reviewer) increase error rates on narrow questions?
- What is the human inter-rater agreement on "the source supports this sentence"? A judge-based metric is only as good as its label definition.

---

## 10. Reproduction

All commands ran on 2026-11-14 in `/work`.

```sh

mkdir -p notes/feynman-evals
curl -sSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Companion-Inc/feynman/main/evals/README.md -o notes/feynman-evals/README.md
curl -sSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Companion-Inc/feynman/main/evals/questions.jsonl -o notes/feynman-evals/questions.jsonl

# result files: https://github.com/Companion-Inc/feynman/tree/main/evals/results

# 2. Build the 13 canaries and run the shipped scorer
cd experiments/feynman-eval-audit
python3 make_canaries.py
cp seed.jsonl seed-input.jsonl
node evals/run.mjs --rescore seed.jsonl

# 3. Run the verifier canary (used the harness's own verifier agent)
#    draft:      experiments/feynman-verifier-canary/draft.md
#    notes:      experiments/feynman-verifier-canary/research-notes.md
#    output:     experiments/feynman-verifier-canary/cited.md
#    log:        experiments/feynman-verifier-canary/verification-log.md
```

content.text:
Done. The case study is at **`outputs/feynman-harness-eval-quality.md`**, with a provenance sidecar at `outputs/feynman-harness-eval-quality.provenance.md`.

## What I actually did

Three probes, all reproducible on disk:

1. **Static audit** of the installed 0.5.65 harness: `SYSTEM.md`, the four agents, `/deepresearch`, and the public `evals/` directory.
2. **Scorer canary suite**: 13 synthetic final outputs with known defects, run through the unmodified `evals/run.mjs --rescore`.
3. **Verifier canary**: a six-claim draft with five seeded defects, run through the harness's own `verifier` agent.

## The core finding

Feynman's product claim is **claim-level verification**. Its public eval measures **identifier-level attribution**: do arXiv/DOI IDs resolve, and does the citing line contain enough title tokens. Those are different constructs.

The scorer results:

| Seeded defect | Detected? |
|---|---|
| Fabricated arXiv ID | yes (`valid = 0%`) |
| Real ID attached to wrong paper title | yes (`title = 0%`) |
| Correct paper, claim contradicted by paper | **no** (100% across all metrics) |
| Fabricated number, no citation | **no** |
| Reference-section citation, contradictory body | **no** |
| PMID-only citation of the key paper | **no** (`recall = 100%`, `cites = 0`) |
| Terse but correct citation | **false positive** (`title = 0%`) |
| Honest disclosure of a removed fake ID | **penalized** (`valid = 75%`) |

Of the nine defect canaries, three were flagged by the validity/title checks; six were not. All 13 canaries — including the zero-citation and false-claim documents — scored `done = yes`.

The verifier canary, by contrast, addressed all five seeded defects, preserved the control, and replaced the fabricated numbers with figures I checked against the arXiv abstracts.

## Eval-hygiene findings

- **4 of 12 questions** have ever been run (33%); only q01/q04/q07/q10.
- **14/14 rows** from the 0.5.2/0.5.3 runs record `git_dirty: true`; the headline 0.5.3 result is not tied to a clean commit.
- **All cost values are `$0`**, because the provider entry had no cost block — the column reads like a measurement but isn't.
- **The public eval ledger stops at 2026-09-24**; the installed version is 0.5.65 (2026-11-06).
- **Refusals are scored as research failures**: Opus 5.5 refusing CRISPR questions becomes `done: false`, `recall: 0%`.
- The release note's "0.5.2: 43 of 43 citations" actually matches the file recorded as **0.5.0** (`d926547`), not either 0.5.2-labelled file.

## Honest caveats

The canaries are synthetic unit tests of the scorer, not population estimates. The verifier canary is n=1, one model, a 103-word draft with blatant defects, and the research notes pre-flagged two of them. It shows the contract works; it does not estimate a catch rate. I did not run a full `/lit` or `/deepresearch` session.

The constructive version: the harness's verification layer is better than its eval can see. The fix is a claim-level entailment lane plus denominators and separated failure statuses — not a bigger version of the same identifier check.

**Reproduction:** `experiments/feynman-eval-audit/make_canaries.py` and `experiments/feynman-verifier-canary/`; full source list is in the artifact.
